item.content:encoded:
South Africa In Southern Africa: Strategies for Responding to the Challenges of Anti-Foreigner Violence

发布源: South African Institute of International Affairs (SAIIA)--South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

In his five-point plan to combat illegal migration and anti-foreigner mobilisation, announced in June this year, President Cyril Ramaphosa included the proposal to work with other African countries, increasing ‘cooperation and engagement with regional partners and continental neighbours to address the broader structural drivers and regional realities of migration’. What could this mean in practice, and how does it relate to the other four points of the plan?

Prof. Hirsch has been a member of President Cyril Ramaphosa’s Economic Advisory Council since 2019 and is a member of Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana’s G20 Africa Expert Panel. He managed economic policy in the South African Presidency from 2002 to 2012, has represented South African presidents in G20 negotiations and co-chaired the G20 Development Working Group. After an early career in academia and a longer career in the South African government, ending as Deputy Director-General of the Presidency, Hirsch established and directed the Nelson Mandela School of Public Governance at the University of Cape Town between 2012 and 2020.

He was also Research Director for Zambia at the International Growth Centre from 2010 to 2015. Since 2019, he has conducted and led research, mostly on migration governance reform in Africa.

We look forward to your participation.

MICHAEL MORRIS | Democracy thrives on imperfection and persistent argument - Business DayNov 09, 2026

发布源: South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

Political change is probably the most important indicator of any society’s freedom to choose to be different.

As we have just learnt from events on opposite sides of the Atlantic, if political freedom does not automatically confer freedom from error, it remains the best means of delivering what most people decide is the necessary correction.

It’s not very efficient, but efficiency is not the thing.

In an email just a few days ago I told a colleague that I believed “the virtue ofdemocracyis precisely its imperfection”, and that we can all have a go at participating in preserving the imperfection as a guarantee against having to accept that one paramount ideal decided by someone, decides what’s best for everyone.

There is always an ideal, and we all routinely berate voters — other voters — for making what we might think are flawed, mistaken or even stupid choices. But they doubtless think the same of us and our choices.

Democracy’s primary advantage (the primary advantage of free societies) is that nobody is ever completely happy, and so the argument persists. And, as I said to my colleague, “if the argument persists, the freedom usually does too”.

(It often strikes me that participating is what’s most meaningful, in the sense that we take part without anticipating that we will automatically get our way and so jointly agree in advance to voluntarily surrendering a great deal of authority to whoever is actually chosen.)

item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
The Hoernlé Memorial Lectures

发布源: South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

The inaugural Hoernlé lecture was delivered by Jan Hendrik Hofmeyr, IRR vice-president and honorary life member, in 1945 on the topic of “Christian principles and race problems”. Other distinguished speakers included IRR co-founder Professor Edgar Brookes on the Institute’s first 21 years in “We come of age” (1950), Archbishop Dennis Hurley on “Apartheid: A crisis of the Christian conscience” (1964), Chief Mangosuthu Buthelezi on “White and black nationalism, ethnicity and the future of the homelands” (1974), Dr Alan Paton on “Towards racial justice: Will there be a change of heart?” (1979) and again on “Federation or desolation” (1985) – the only speaker to have delivered two Hoernlé lectures – Professor Jonathan Jansen on “When does a university cease to exist?” (2005) and Professor RW Johnson on “The future of the liberal tradition in South Africa” (2011).

The speakers often tackled thorny questions relating to race, ideology and South Africa’s future. In their explorations, they reflected the most pressing preoccupations of their times, giving us a window into the past that shows contemporary views on issues that often seemed intractable at the time. It is sobering to look back from today’s vantage point and realise how far South Africa has come – and how much still remains to be done to create a free and prosperous South Africa for all.

item.content:encoded:
History of the IRR Bursary Programme (1936-2022)

发布源: South African Institute of Race Relations (IRR) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

From a time of simple racial segregation in the first part of the twentieth century, through the intensified racial regime of the apartheid period and for nearly three decades into post-apartheid democracy, about 6,000 black South Africans graduated from universities, technikons and other tertiary institutions thanks to the bursary programme administered by the South African Institute of Race Relations (SAIRR). Immense hurdles had to be overcome, both by the students themselves as well as funders and administrators.

While unquestionably delivering positive outcomes, the programme was often caught up in the turbulence of the times, especially during the popular resistance from the mid-1970s to the early 1990s. If not itself the subject of controversy, it was often linked to controversy and conflict around matters like reform versus revolution, disinvestment versus business influence, and armed struggle versus peaceful resistance. This is the story of that bursary programme and the tumultuous times in which it operated.

The South African Institute of Race Relations (SAIRR) is a classically liberal not-for-profit organisation, founded in 1929 with the objective of improving relations between South Africa's race groups. This almost immediately became a matter of opposing racial discrimination and promoting the establishment of a non-racial society in South Africa. item.content:encoded:
African Heritage Program

发布源: Mandela Institute for Development Studies (MINDS) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

CULTURE AND DEVELOPMENT

The African Heritage Program explores African people, culture and heritage to ground development in Africanness. Through rigorous research, it deepens the understanding of African identity and value systems to inform development practice.

FOUNDATIONAL APPROACH

MINDS believes that a better understanding of Africanness begins with systematic research and rigorous analysis of African heritage. This work seeks to develop an inclusive conceptualisation of Africanness, grounded in the values,and lived realities of African societies. Anchored in this understanding, the programme aims to inform development initiatives that are culturally grounded and more effective in addressing Africa’s development challenges.

APPLYING KNOWLEDGE

The Program identifies foundational African principles across governance, leadership and knowledge domains, applying these insights to assess and shape development initiatives.

item.content:encoded:
Economic Integration Program

发布源: Mandela Institute for Development Studies (MINDS) --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

REGIONAL COOPERATION

Accelerating Africa’s growth requires stronger cross-sector partnerships and deeper regional integration.

PROGRAM RESPONSE

Through the Economic Integration Program, MINDS underscores the urgency of advancing integration as a driver of Africa’s development. Despite strong continental intent, fragmented markets persist, limiting growth. The program promotes practical implementation, strengthens regional value chains, and improves market access to support the shift from policy ambition to meaningful, sustained economic transformation.

APPLYING KNOWLEDGE

Through inclusive, multi-sectoral dialogues, the MINDS High-Level Dialogue Series strengthens relationships across Africa, helping leaders from all sectors create shared visions and work together to tackle the continent’s complex development issues.

TheAfrican Centre for Cities(University of Cape Town) and theUrban School of Sciences Po(Paris) two highly rated institutions in Urban Studies worldwide, are launching a new collaborative master’s degree programme to begin in January 2027. The joint master’s draws on synergies between the two universities in cutting-edge interdisciplinary training in urban governance and urban policy. It provides students with the enriching experience and on-the-ground training in two dynamic global cities. Students spend their first semester in Cape Town, the second year in Paris, and return to Cape Town for the final semester of the programme.

The MPhil in African and Southern Urban Studies offers a unique opportunity to engage critically with the dynamics of urbanisation from the perspective of the Global South, with a strong focus on research. The programme combines rigorous academic training and applied learning in Cape Town and Paris — two urban laboratories facing complex development challenges.

The programme provides advanced interdisciplinary training in Southern urban theory and everyday urban life. Drawing on grounded, context-rich research and the vibrant intellectual environment of both institutions, students are placed at the intersection of theory, policy, and practice. They also have the opportunity to pursue fieldwork, internships, or capstone projects during their time in Cape Town and Paris.

item.description: 网站专栏报告。作者: 智库研究员。这篇智库文章初次发表在Africa Centre for Cities --South Africa官方网站上。
item.content:encoded:
MPhil in Urban Studies — Southern Urbanism

发布源: Africa Centre for Cities --South Africa | 抓取时间: 2026-11-12

It is well known that the world is transitioning to an irrevocable urban future whose epicentre has moved into the cities of Asia and Africa, which together will account for 86% of all growth in the world’s urban population over the next four decades.

This unprecedented increase will pose new environmental, economic and social challenges, the full implications of which demand new understandings as city-making and remaking are entangled in these vast multi-dimensional shifts. These shifts also highlight a profound crisis of knowledge production, one that forces us to question taken-for-granted assumptions of the field of Urban Studies. What is needed is critical engagement with the dominant Global North theories, bold methodological experimentation, plural perspectives brought into conversation through co-production  and critical inquiry from a Global South perspective that resists easy generalisations.

If you are interested in taking up this challenge, theMPhil in Southern Urbanismis your learning platform. Through a combination of guided learning in small-group seminars, experimentation in various spaces of urban practice and  independent thesis research, the programme provides a truly unique opportunity to ground yourself in the realities, theories and practise of cities of the Global South.

The MPhil curriculum combines course work (50%) and a minor dissertation (50%), a full-time load completed overa period of 24 months.The language of instruction is English.
